participant.bigIdea: Agile analysis is not a lighter BA — it is the same discipline applied at the right horizon, at the right time.
participant.overview:
Welcome to Agile Business Analysis. Over two days you will work through the whole Agile Extension to the BABOK Guide — Chapters 1 to 9 — in eight teaching sessions and two applied exercises. Day 1 builds the foundations: what agile business analysis actually is, the mindset and principles behind it, the Three Planning Horizons and the people who make up an agile product team. Day 2 goes horizon by horizon and then into practice: events, scaling, common challenges and the competencies an agile business analyst (ABA) needs.

Throughout both days we use a single running case: **Faster grant payments for community organisations**, an illustrative government digital-service scenario at the fictional Department of Community Services. Today a community group waits on average 46 days from submitting a small-grant application through Community Grants Online to receiving funds; the target is 20 days or fewer within twelve months. You will see that one outcome analysed at strategy, initiative and delivery level, so the horizons stop being abstract. Along the way, side examples from technology, healthcare, sport, higher education and other industries show the same techniques travelling.

sections.heading: How the guide is organised
sections.body:
The Agile Extension is organised around a simple idea: business analysis happens continuously, at different levels of detail, for different decisions. The chapters move from **why** (introduction and context), to **how we think** (the mindset and its principles), to **where we work** (the Three Planning Horizons), to **how we do it** (techniques, events, scaling and competencies).

| Course session | Guide focus |
|---|---|
| 1A | What agile analysis is · project vs product thinking |
| 1B | The agile analysis mindset · BACCM · nine principles |
| 2A | The Three Planning Horizons |
| 2B | The agile product team and the ABA role |
| 3A | The Strategy Horizon |
| 3B | The Initiative and Delivery Horizons |
| 4A | Agile events · analysis across horizons · scaling |
| 4B | Common challenges · underlying competencies |

sections.heading: The running case
sections.body:
**Faster grant payments for community organisations.** Community organisations applying to the Department of Community Services' Community Grants Online platform currently wait an average of 46 days between submitting a small-grant application (up to $15,000) and receiving funds. Around a third of helpdesk enquiries are applicants asking where their application is, and delays push volunteer-run projects past their start dates. The department wants submission-to-payment at **20 days or fewer within twelve months**, and application-status enquiries down 40%.

We use this case because it has a clear measurable outcome, several stakeholder groups with competing interests (community organisations, auspice bodies, regional assessment officers, finance and probity teams, the Minister's office, sector peak bodies), public-sector governance, privacy, procurement and accessibility constraints, and a mix of process, data and technology change — exactly the conditions where agile analysis earns its keep.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

sections.body:

- **Bring your own initiative.** Each activity has a box for the course case and, where useful, your own work. Real context makes the learning stick.
- **Timeboxes are real.** We practise what we preach: when the timer ends, we inspect and adapt.
- **Paraphrase, don't recite.** We discuss the guide's ideas in our own words; the goal is application, not memorisation.

modules.title: What agile business analysis is
modules.subtitle: Project vs product · why analysis still matters when we go agile

participant.bigIdea: Agile analysis exists to keep a team building the right thing — continuously, not once.
participant.overview:
Many organisations adopt agile delivery and quietly assume business analysis disappears with the requirements document. The opposite is true. When teams deliver in small increments, decisions about *what* to build next happen every week rather than once a year — and each one needs analysis: understanding the need, framing options, and checking whether the last change delivered value.

This session defines agile business analysis, separates it from simply 'doing BA work on an agile project', and contrasts project thinking with product thinking. We use the first-payment case to show how the same outcome looks very different when framed as a project with a fixed scope versus a product with a measurable outcome.
objectives: Define agile business analysis in your own words
Contrast project-oriented and product-oriented ways of working
Explain why fast feedback changes when and how analysis is done
Reframe a scope-based initiative as an outcome-based one

keyPoints.title: Analysis is continuous
keyPoints.body: In agile settings analysis is spread across the whole life of a product, done just enough and just in time for the decision at hand.

keyPoints.title: Value over output
keyPoints.body: Success is measured by change in the customer's situation (days to receive funds), not by features shipped.

keyPoints.title: Projects end; products persist
keyPoints.body: A project optimises for delivering scope on time. A product optimises for outcomes over its whole life, with a stable team learning as it goes.

keyPoints.title: Anyone can do analysis
keyPoints.body: Agile analysis is a set of activities, not a job title. The ABA often coaches others to do it well.

sections.heading: What makes analysis 'agile'
sections.body:
Agile business analysis is business analysis performed in a context where change is expected and feedback is fast. Three things distinguish it:

1. **Timing.** Analysis is done when a decision needs to be made, not in a front-loaded phase. Detail is elaborated progressively — broad at the start, specific only for the work about to be built.
2. **Granularity.** Work is sliced into small, valuable increments, each of which can be tested with real users or data.
3. **Feedback as input.** Every increment produces evidence. The analyst's job includes reading that evidence and recommending whether to persevere, pivot or stop.

None of this abandons rigour. It moves rigour from documentation to decisions: clear hypotheses, explicit assumptions, measurable outcomes and visible trade-offs.

sections.heading: Project thinking vs product thinking
sections.body:
| Dimension | Project thinking | Product thinking |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of funding | A scope of work with a budget and end date | A persistent team funded to move an outcome |
| Success measure | On time, on budget, scope delivered | Measurable change in customer or business outcome |
| Requirements | Agreed and baselined early | Emergent; prioritised continuously |
| Change | Controlled through change requests | Expected; absorbed through backlog reprioritisation |
| Team | Assembled, then disbanded | Stable and long-lived; knowledge retained |
| Analyst's focus | Completeness of specification | Quality of the next decision |

Most organisations sit somewhere in between. A common hybrid is project funding wrapped around product-style delivery teams. The ABA needs to recognise which logic is driving decisions — because a project governance board will ask 'is the scope done?' when the real question is 'has the outcome moved?'

sections.heading: The case through both lenses
sections.body:
**As a project:** 'Deliver a new online grants portal with integration to the finance system by 30 June, budget $3.4m.' Success is the portal going live.

**As a product:** 'Reduce submission-to-payment for small grants from 46 to ≤20 days within 12 months.' The portal is one *possible* means. Analysis might show that the biggest delay is not submission at all but the default wait for auspice bodies to confirm sponsorship before assessment starts, or missing certificates of currency for public liability insurance. A product team would test the cheapest intervention first — perhaps asking the auspice body to confirm in parallel with assessment — and measure the effect within weeks.

The product framing makes the analyst's contribution visible: identifying where time is actually lost and which change would move the number most. The same shift applies elsewhere: a SaaS company reframing 'ship the new onboarding wizard' as 'cut time-to-first-value for new customers by half'.

sections.heading: Where agile analysis applies
sections.body: Agile analysis is not confined to software. It applies wherever you can deliver change in small increments and observe the result: policy pilots, process redesign, service design, data products. It is less suited to work where an increment cannot be released or tested — but even there, the mindset (explicit assumptions, early feedback, value focus) improves outcomes.

participant.bigIdea: Techniques are borrowed; mindset is what makes them agile.
participant.overview:
Two analysts can run the same user story workshop and get very different results. The difference is mindset: what they believe the work is for, how they treat uncertainty and how they respond to evidence. The Agile Extension describes an agile analysis mindset expressed through a set of principles, and grounds it in the Business Analysis Core Concept Model (BACCM) — the six concepts that frame all business analysis.

In this session you will connect the BACCM to agile practice, work through the nine principles in plain language, and test them against the running case. The principles are not a checklist; they are a lens for deciding what to do when the guide doesn't tell you.
objectives: Describe the six BACCM concepts and how each shows up in agile work
Explain the nine principles in your own words with an example of each
Diagnose which principles are weak in a given situation
Apply the principles to choose an analysis approach for the case

keyPoints.title: BACCM is the backbone
keyPoints.body: Change, Need, Solution, Stakeholder, Value and Context — every analysis decision touches all six.

keyPoints.title: Principles over procedures
keyPoints.body: When there is no prescribed step, the principles tell you what good looks like.

keyPoints.title: Uncertainty is information
keyPoints.body: An agile analyst makes uncertainty explicit and reduces it deliberately through experiments.

keyPoints.title: Value is judged, then verified
keyPoints.body: Value is estimated up front and measured after delivery; both matter.

sections.heading: The BACCM in an agile setting
sections.body:
| Concept | Plain meaning | Agile emphasis | In the case |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Change** | The act of transforming in response to a need | Small, frequent, reversible changes | Parallel auspice confirmation trialled in one region |
| **Need** | A problem or opportunity | Re-validated as evidence arrives | Community groups waiting 46 days for funds |
| **Solution** | A way of satisfying needs | One of several options; tested, not assumed | Parallel confirmation, triage, portal, status updates |
| **Stakeholder** | Anyone with a relationship to the change | Engaged continuously, not at sign-off | Applicants, auspice bodies, assessors, finance, probity, peak bodies |
| **Value** | Worth or usefulness to a stakeholder | Measured after each increment | Days saved; enquiries avoided; projects starting on time |
| **Context** | Circumstances that influence the change | Constraints made visible early | Grants guidelines, probity rules, accessibility standards |

The model is useful as a quick completeness check: if a backlog item cannot be traced to a need, a stakeholder and a measure of value, it is a candidate for removal — whether you are building a grants platform or a hospital's telehealth booking flow.

sections.heading: The nine principles, in plain language
sections.body:
The guide groups its mindset into principles. In this course we work with nine, paraphrased for practice:

1. **See the whole.** Understand the broader system — customers, operations, policy — before optimising a part.
2. **Think as a customer.** Frame needs from the perspective of the person who experiences the outcome.
3. **Analyse to determine what is valuable.** Continually assess which work would deliver the most value next.
4. **Get real using examples.** Make needs concrete through scenarios, examples and acceptance criteria.
5. **Understand what is doable.** Work within real constraints — capability, capacity, regulation — and expose them early.
6. **Stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement.** Create conditions for shared understanding and inspect-and-adapt.
7. **Avoid waste.** Do only the analysis needed for the next decision; drop work that adds no value.
8. **Embrace uncertainty.** Treat unknowns as testable assumptions rather than risks to be documented away.
9. **Deliver value continuously.** Prefer small increments that can be measured over large batches.

Principles 1–4 lean toward *understanding*, 5–7 toward *working together sensibly*, and 8–9 toward *learning and flow*.

sections.heading: Principles in tension
sections.body:
Principles conflict. 'Avoid waste' can argue against the stakeholder workshop that 'See the whole' demands. 'Embrace uncertainty' can collide with a regulator who needs certainty about statutory compliance. The ABA's job is to make the tension explicit and pick a deliberate trade-off.

In the case, Legal may require a complete map of statutory timeframes before any process change. That looks like big up-front analysis — but it is the *right* amount for a compliance-critical constraint. Doing it is consistent with 'Understand what is doable'. The waste would be extending that same depth to every UI detail of a future portal.

sections.heading: Diagnosing a weak mindset
sections.body:
Symptoms that a team's mindset has drifted:

- Stories describe system behaviour but no user or outcome (*Think as a customer* is weak).
- The backlog has 400 items and nobody can say which matter most (*Analyse to determine what is valuable*).
- Acceptance criteria are 'works as expected' (*Get real using examples*).
- Releases are quarterly despite two-week sprints (*Deliver value continuously*).
- Assumptions are buried in a risk register nobody reads (*Embrace uncertainty*).

modules.title: The Three Planning Horizons
modules.subtitle: Strategy · Initiative · Delivery — and how they connect

participant.bigIdea: Every analysis question belongs to a horizon; answer it at the wrong one and you waste effort or miss the point.
participant.overview:
The heart of the Agile Extension is the Three Planning Horizons model. Organisations make decisions at different cadences and levels of detail: long-range strategic choices, medium-range initiative choices, and short-range delivery choices. Business analysis happens at all three, with different questions, stakeholders, techniques and feedback loops.

This session introduces the model, shows how feedback flows up as well as decisions flowing down, and maps the running case across the three horizons. By the end you will be able to place any analysis request on the right horizon — the single most useful diagnostic in the course.
objectives: Describe the purpose, cadence and typical decisions of each horizon
Explain how decisions cascade down and feedback flows up
Place analysis questions on the correct horizon
Map the running case across all three horizons

keyPoints.title: Strategy
keyPoints.body: Long cadence (often 6–18 months). Why and where: direction, investment, outcomes. Feedback is slow and broad.

keyPoints.title: Initiative
keyPoints.body: Medium cadence (weeks to months). What: the solution approach and capabilities to achieve a strategic outcome.

keyPoints.title: Delivery
keyPoints.body: Short cadence (days to weeks). How, in detail: the increments a team builds and validates.

keyPoints.title: Two-way flow
keyPoints.body: Decisions cascade down; evidence flows up. A horizon that never receives feedback is planning in a vacuum.

sections.heading: The model at a glance
sections.body:
| | Strategy Horizon | Initiative Horizon | Delivery Horizon |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core question | Why are we doing this, and where should we invest? | What solution approach will achieve the goal? | How exactly do we build and validate the next increment? |
| Typical cadence | Quarterly to annual | Monthly to quarterly | Daily to fortnightly |
| Decision makers | Executives, portfolio boards | Product owners, initiative leads | Delivery team, product owner |
| Analysis outputs | Goals, outcomes, business model, options | Capability maps, story maps, release hypotheses, MVP | Stories, examples, acceptance criteria, models |
| Feedback signals | Market and outcome trends | Adoption and outcome leading indicators | Working software, test results, user reactions |

The horizons are not phases: all three run concurrently. A strategy decision made in March is still live while a team delivers in June.

sections.heading: Cascade and feedback
sections.body:
Decisions flow **down**: strategy sets outcomes and guardrails; initiatives choose approaches that serve them; delivery slices those approaches into increments.

Evidence flows **up**: delivery learns that a validation rule is far harder than estimated; the initiative re-plans its MVP; strategy learns that the seven-day target needs a policy change, not just a system.

The ABA is often the person who makes sure feedback actually travels upward. Without that, strategy ossifies and teams deliver faithfully toward a target that the evidence says is unreachable.

sections.heading: The case across the horizons
sections.body:
**Strategy:** Strengthen community programs by getting grant funds to organisations faster. Outcome: submission to payment ≤20 days within 12 months; application-status enquiries −40%. Investment envelope and option choice (e.g. buy a grants-management platform through a panel procurement, integrate via middleware).

**Initiative:** 'Digital application and streamlined approval for low-risk small grants.' Capabilities: accessible online application, parallel auspice confirmation, document validation, risk triage. MVP hypothesis: *if* applicants submit online and auspice bodies confirm in parallel, *then* average time to payment for low-risk grants will fall below 30 days within one quarter.

**Delivery:** 'As a community organisation applicant, I want to upload our certificate of currency when I apply, so that our application isn't held up waiting for it.' Examples: a valid PDF certificate; a photo; a certificate with an expired date; no certificate.

sections.heading: Placing questions on a horizon
sections.body:
A quick test: ask **how long it would take to learn whether the answer was right.**

- Years or many months → Strategy.
- Weeks to a quarter → Initiative.
- Days to a sprint → Delivery.

Requests are often asked at the wrong horizon: an executive asking 'what fields should the form have?' (delivery question at strategy level) or a team asked to 'just build the portal' without a defined outcome (strategy question left unanswered).

modules.title: The agile product team and the ABA
modules.subtitle: Roles, responsibilities and where analysis lives

participant.bigIdea: Analysis is a team responsibility; the ABA makes sure it's done well and done at the right horizon.
participant.overview:
Agile frameworks rarely name a 'business analyst'. Scrum has a product owner, developers and a scrum master; other frameworks add roles such as product manager or release train engineer. That absence makes some BAs anxious and leads some organisations to remove the role entirely. The Agile Extension takes a different view: analysis is a set of activities the whole team needs, and someone with strong analysis capability — the agile business analyst — adds enormous value whether or not that is their title.

This session looks at the agile product team, the ways the ABA contributes alongside or as part of the product owner role, and how the ABA's focus shifts across horizons.
objectives: Describe the common roles in an agile product team
Explain several ways the ABA role can be structured
Distinguish the product owner's accountability from the ABA's contribution
Define your own ABA contribution for the case and your initiative

keyPoints.title: Accountability vs activity
keyPoints.body: The product owner is accountable for value and backlog order. Analysis activities that inform those decisions can be done by an ABA, the PO, or the team.

keyPoints.title: Several valid shapes
keyPoints.body: ABA as product owner, as proxy, as team member, or as an analyst serving several teams — each with trade-offs.

keyPoints.title: Horizon shifts the role
keyPoints.body: At strategy the ABA looks like a business architect; at delivery like an embedded analyst writing examples with testers.

keyPoints.title: Coach, not gatekeeper
keyPoints.body: A strong ABA spreads analysis capability through the team rather than becoming a bottleneck.

sections.heading: Who's on an agile product team
sections.body:
| Role | Core accountability | Where analysis shows up |
|---|---|---|
| Product owner / product manager | Maximise value; own the backlog order | Prioritisation, outcome definition, stakeholder trade-offs |
| Developers (incl. testers, designers) | Build a usable, valuable increment | Refining stories, examples, technical feasibility |
| Scrum master / agile coach | Effective process and team health | Facilitating refinement, retrospectives |
| Agile business analyst | Shared understanding of needs and value | Elicitation, modelling, slicing, hypothesis framing, measuring value |
| Stakeholders and customers | Provide needs and feedback | Reviews, testing, discovery interviews |

sections.heading: Shapes the ABA role can take
sections.body:
1. **ABA as product owner.** One person holds accountability and does the analysis. Clear, but the PO needs real decision authority — an analyst 'PO' without it becomes a proxy in disguise.
2. **ABA supporting a product owner.** The PO decides; the ABA researches, models and prepares options. Works well when the PO is a busy business leader.
3. **ABA as team member.** Analysis is one skill within a cross-functional team; the ABA also tests, facilitates or designs.
4. **ABA across teams.** One analyst supports several teams on a shared product, often at initiative horizon, ensuring consistency of capabilities and data.

No shape is universally right. Choose based on where the PO's capacity gaps are and how complex the stakeholder landscape is.

sections.heading: The ABA across horizons
sections.body:
- **Strategy:** helps leaders articulate outcomes, compare options, test business model assumptions. Partners with enterprise and business architects.
- **Initiative:** shapes the solution approach: capability maps, story maps, MVP and release hypotheses, stakeholder alignment.
- **Delivery:** works with the team on story slicing, examples, acceptance criteria, lightweight models, and checking delivered value.

In the case, one ABA might spend Monday helping the Director of Grants Operations frame the twenty-day outcome for the executive board, Wednesday building the story map for online applications, and Thursday writing examples for certificate upload with a tester. Moving between horizons — and carrying insight between them — is the role's distinctive value. A university ABA might do the same across an enrolment redesign: framing the outcome with the Registrar, mapping the student journey, then refining stories with the LMS team.

sections.heading: Anti-patterns
sections.body:
- **Requirements handover.** The ABA writes stories in isolation and throws them to the team. Fix: co-write in refinement.
- **Proxy without power.** The ABA is called PO but every decision escalates. Fix: make decision rights explicit.
- **Bottleneck analyst.** Nothing enters a sprint without the ABA. Fix: coach the team to write examples; review rather than author.
- **Delivery-only BA.** The analyst never sees strategy, so can't judge value. Fix: secure a seat at initiative reviews.

modules.title: The Strategy Horizon
modules.subtitle: Analysing goals, outcomes and options at the top of the map

participant.bigIdea: At the strategy horizon, the ABA's job is to make the bet explicit — and testable.
participant.overview:
Strategy horizon analysis supports the organisation's longest-range decisions: which outcomes matter, where to invest and which business model or service assumptions to test. Feedback is slow, stakes are high and stakeholders are senior. Agile analysis contributes by converting strategy statements into measurable outcomes, surfacing the riskiest assumptions and framing investment as a series of options rather than a single commitment.

We work through the case's strategy horizon: from 'strengthen community programs' to a measurable outcome, an assumption map, and an options comparison.
objectives: Describe the purpose and stakeholders of strategy horizon analysis
Translate a strategic intent into measurable outcomes with leading indicators
Identify and rank the riskiest strategic assumptions
Compare investment options using value, risk and learning speed

keyPoints.title: Intent → outcome
keyPoints.body: Strategic intent becomes an outcome with baseline, target, timeframe, guardrails and leading indicators.

keyPoints.title: Assumptions are the risk
keyPoints.body: Every strategy rests on beliefs. Rank them by impact and uncertainty; test the top-right first.

keyPoints.title: Options, not a plan
keyPoints.body: Frame investment as staged options with decision points that evidence can trigger.

keyPoints.title: Typical techniques
keyPoints.body: Business model canvas, value stream mapping, purpose alignment, impact mapping, assumption mapping, Kano and real options thinking.

sections.heading: What happens at the strategy horizon
sections.body:
Strategy horizon analysis answers: *why change, where to play, and how will we know it worked?* Typical inputs are corporate plans, regulatory direction, customer research and performance data. Outputs include outcome statements, investment themes, option assessments and the guardrails within which initiatives operate.

Cadence is long — quarterly or annual planning, with occasional off-cycle pivots. The ABA's distinctive contribution is to keep strategy honest: anchor it in evidence, make assumptions visible, and design leading indicators so the organisation doesn't wait a year to learn it was wrong.

sections.heading: From intent to outcome
sections.body:
**Intent:** 'Help community organisations deliver their projects on time by getting grant funds to them sooner.'

| Element | Case example |
|---|---|
| Outcome | Average submission-to-payment ≤20 days |
| Baseline | 46 days (illustrative) |
| Timeframe | Within 12 months |
| Supporting measure | Application-status enquiries −40% |
| Guardrails | No increase in grants approved outside guidelines; probity findings not worse |
| Leading indicators | % applications with valid certificate at submission; % auspice bodies confirming within 2 days; median days by risk tier |

Leading indicators move within weeks and predict the lagging outcome — they are what lets strategy receive feedback quickly. A professional sports club does the same when it tracks weekly membership renewals as a leading indicator of season revenue.

sections.heading: Assumption mapping
sections.body:
Plot assumptions on two axes: **impact if wrong** and **current evidence**. High-impact, low-evidence assumptions are tested first.

Case assumptions:
- A large share of small-grant applications is genuinely low-risk and suitable for streamlined approval. *(High impact, low evidence — test first via historical data analysis.)*
- The auspice confirmation wait is the largest single delay. *(High impact, medium evidence — validate with timestamp analysis.)*
- Volunteer-run organisations will apply online if offered an accessible digital channel. *(Medium impact, low evidence — test via pilot.)*
- Regional assessors will accept process change without KPI changes. *(High impact, low evidence — test via stakeholder interviews.)*

sections.heading: Comparing options
sections.body:
| Option | Description | Value potential | Risk | Speed to learn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Expand helpdesk to chase applications | Low (treats symptom) | Low | Fast |
| B | Buy a grants-management platform via panel procurement, integrate via middleware; phased MVP | High | Medium | Medium |
| C | Build bespoke end-to-end grants system | High | High | Slow |
| D | Policy and process change only (parallel auspice confirmation, triage) | Medium | Low | Fast |

A strong recommendation often combines options: start D immediately to learn fast and bank early value, while staging B with a decision point after the MVP. That is real-options thinking — buy the right, not the obligation, to invest further.

modules.title: Initiative and Delivery Horizons
modules.subtitle: From solution approach to stories with examples

participant.bigIdea: The initiative horizon decides what to build first; the delivery horizon makes it unambiguous.
participant.overview:
Once strategy sets the outcome, the initiative horizon shapes a solution approach: the capabilities required, the minimum viable product and the release plan expressed as hypotheses. The delivery horizon then turns the next slice into small, testable work items with concrete examples.

This session covers both, because the hand-off between them is where many agile teams lose value. We build a story map for online grant applications, define the MVP, and write delivery-ready stories with examples and acceptance criteria.
objectives: Explain the purpose and outputs of initiative and delivery horizon analysis
Build a story map and slice an MVP
Write stories with concrete examples and acceptance criteria
Choose appropriate techniques for each horizon

keyPoints.title: Initiative: shape the solution
keyPoints.body: Capabilities, story maps, MVP and release hypotheses. Cadence: weeks to a quarter.

keyPoints.title: Delivery: make it concrete
keyPoints.body: Stories, examples, acceptance criteria and lightweight models — done just before the work is pulled.

keyPoints.title: Story maps bridge both
keyPoints.body: The backbone is initiative-level; the slices below become delivery backlog.

keyPoints.title: Examples are the specification
keyPoints.body: Concrete examples remove ambiguity faster than prose and double as tests.

sections.heading: Initiative horizon analysis
sections.body:
Initiative analysis answers *what solution, delivered in what order, will move the outcome?* Typical activities:

- **Capability and context mapping** to understand what must change.
- **Stakeholder analysis** for the initiative's specific landscape.
- **Story mapping** to lay out the user journey and slice releases.
- **MVP definition** — the smallest release that tests the riskiest hypothesis.
- **Release hypotheses** — each release has an expected measurable effect.

Techniques the guide associates here include story mapping, impact mapping, personas, journey mapping, value modelling and minimal viable product thinking.

sections.heading: Story map for online grant applications
sections.body:
**Backbone (applicant journey):** Find grant → Submit application → Provide evidence → Auspice confirms → Application assessed → Receive funds → Track status

| Release | Slice | Hypothesis |
|---|---|---|
| MVP | Applicant applies online; uploads certificate; auspice body emailed in parallel; manual triage | Low-risk grants reach payment in <30 days |
| R2 | Automated certificate checks; rule-based low-risk triage | Low-risk grants <20 days; assessor effort per application −20% |
| R3 | Proactive SMS status; auspice portal confirmation | Application-status enquiries −40% |

The MVP is deliberately unglamorous: manual triage behind a simple, accessible digital front end. It tests the biggest assumption (parallel confirmation shortens time) before investing in automation.

sections.heading: Delivery horizon analysis
sections.body:
Delivery analysis answers *exactly what does this increment do, and how will we know it's done?* It happens in refinement, just before the work is pulled, with the people who will build and test it.

**Story:** As a community organisation applicant, I want to upload our certificate of currency when I apply, so that our application isn't held up waiting for it.

**Examples (specification by example):**

| Given | When | Then |
|---|---|---|
| A valid PDF certificate current for at least 30 days | Applicant uploads at submission | Certificate is attached and status shows 'Received' |
| A clear phone photo of a certificate | Applicant uploads | Accepted and flagged for assessor visual check |
| A certificate whose cover period has expired | Applicant uploads | Applicant is told it has expired and how to get a current one; submission can continue |
| No certificate | Applicant submits | Submission succeeds; applicant receives a reminder with guidance within 24 hours |

Notice the third and fourth rows: submission is never blocked, because blocking would slow the outcome. That design choice came from the strategy-level guardrail and outcome — the horizons connecting.

sections.heading: Slicing well
sections.body: Good slices are **vertical** (deliver a thin end-to-end piece of value), **independent** where possible, and **testable**. Useful slicing patterns: by workflow step, by business rule variation, by data variation, by happy path vs exceptions, by user type. Avoid horizontal slices ('build the database', 'build the UI') that deliver no value alone.

activities.title: Extend the story map
activities.instructions: In groups, add two activities under each backbone step for the MVP and R2. Then challenge the MVP: is there an even smaller slice that would test the hypothesis?

activities.title: Stories with examples
activities.instructions: Write two delivery stories for the case (e.g. parallel auspice confirmation; low-risk triage flag) with at least three Given/When/Then examples each, including one exception.

participant.aiPrompt: Here is a user story: [paste]. Generate 6 Given/When/Then examples covering the happy path, at least two business-rule variations and two exceptions. Then identify any ambiguous words in the story and list the questions I should ask the product owner. Don't invent business rules — mark them as questions.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the MVP in the case?
opts: Test the riskiest hypothesis with the smallest release
quiz.why: Manual triage behind a simple front end tests parallel notification cheaply.

quiz.q: Which is a vertical slice?
opts: Worker uploads a PDF certificate and sees 'Received'
quiz.why: It delivers end-to-end value.

quiz.q: Why does submission continue when a certificate of currency has expired?
opts: Blocking would slow the outcome; the guardrail is handled by assessor review before approval
quiz.why: Delivery design follows strategic outcome and guardrails.

quiz.q: When does delivery horizon analysis typically happen?
opts: Just before work is pulled, in refinement
quiz.why: Just enough, just in time.

takeaways: Story maps connect initiative and delivery
MVPs test hypotheses, not feature lists
Examples are the clearest specification
Slice vertically

presenter.purpose: Build practical story mapping, MVP and example-writing skills linked to the case outcome.
presenter.openingLine: "Yesterday we wrote 'upload certificate'. Today we find out how many ways that story can go wrong — and why that's the most valuable fifteen minutes of analysis you'll do this sprint."

beats.label: Hook
beats.notes: Ask for ways certificate upload can go wrong; collect five fast.

beats.label: Initiative horizon and story map
beats.notes: Build the backbone live.

beats.label: Activity 1
beats.notes: Groups in breakouts.

beats.label: Delivery horizon and examples
beats.notes: Walk the example table; emphasise the never-block design.

beats.label: Activity 2
beats.notes: Pairs.

beats.label: Slicing patterns and debrief
beats.notes: Share best exception example; review a horizontal slice and fix it together.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Story mapping online works best on a shared board with sticky notes; pre-build the backbone. When groups propose a smaller MVP, celebrate it — e.g. 'email form + manual entry' is a valid MVP. For Activity 2, insist on at least one exception example.
presenter.whatGood: A thinner MVP than the one presented; examples covering exceptions; stories traceable to the hypothesis.
presenter.commonFailure: Examples that restate the story ('Given a user, when they do the thing, then it works') — fix: require concrete data values in each example.
debrief: Did anyone find a smaller MVP?
Which exception example was most revealing?
Where does the initiative-to-delivery handover break in your organisation?
presenter.answerKey:
**Smaller MVP:** a simple accessible web form feeding a shared mailbox, with an automated email to the auspice body and manual assessor entry — tests parallel confirmation in two weeks without integration.

**Story: parallel auspice confirmation.** Given a submitted application with a valid auspice email, when the applicant submits, then the auspice body receives notice within 5 minutes with a link to confirm sponsorship. Given an invalid auspice email, then the assessor is alerted to contact the auspice body by phone within one business day. Given the auspice body confirms within 2 days, then the application is marked 'Auspice confirmed' and the assessor proceeds.

**Story: low-risk triage flag.** Given a program on the low-risk list, a request under $15,000 and a valid certificate, then the application is flagged low-risk. Given a project involving work with children or vulnerable people, then it is never auto-flagged. Given missing auspice details, then not flagged until confirmed.

modules.title: Agile events, across horizons, and scaling
modules.subtitle: Where analysis happens in the cadence — and what changes at scale

participant.bigIdea: Analysis has a rhythm; get into the events and you get into the decisions.
participant.overview: Agile work runs on recurring events — planning, refinement, reviews, retrospectives — and larger organisations add events for coordinating many teams. The ABA's influence depends on knowing what each event is for and what analysis it needs. This session maps analysis to events at each horizon, explores how analysis carries across horizons, and looks at what changes when you scale to many teams working on one product or portfolio.
objectives: Identify the analysis contribution to common agile events
Map events to horizons
Explain how analysis outputs flow across horizons
Describe analysis challenges and practices at scale

keyPoints.title: Every event has an analysis job
keyPoints.body: Refinement clarifies, planning commits, review gathers evidence, retrospective improves the way analysis is done.

keyPoints.title: Each horizon has its events
keyPoints.body: Delivery: sprint events. Initiative: release/quarterly planning, roadmap review. Strategy: portfolio and strategy reviews.

keyPoints.title: Scale adds coordination
keyPoints.body: More teams means shared backlogs, dependencies and consistent definitions — analysis becomes a connective function.

keyPoints.title: Frameworks differ; needs don't
keyPoints.body: Whatever the scaling framework, someone must keep needs, value and dependencies coherent.

sections.heading: Analysis in delivery events
sections.body:
| Event | Purpose | ABA contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Backlog refinement | Make upcoming work ready | Slicing, examples, open questions, dependency checks |
| Sprint planning | Commit to a goal and work | Clarify goal against outcome; confirm readiness |
| Daily stand-up | Coordinate | Unblock questions quickly; avoid analysis queues |
| Sprint review | Inspect increment with stakeholders | Prepare evidence: did it move the indicator? Capture feedback as backlog changes |
| Retrospective | Improve how we work | Raise analysis-related impediments |

sections.heading: Events at initiative and strategy horizons
sections.body:
- **Initiative:** quarterly or release planning (choose the next release hypothesis), roadmap reviews, MVP results reviews (persevere, pivot, stop), stakeholder showcases.
- **Strategy:** portfolio reviews, outcome reviews, investment decisions, strategy refreshes.

In the case: a fortnightly sprint review shows auspice notification working; a monthly initiative review examines days-to-payment by risk tier; a quarterly steering review checks the ≤20-day trajectory and guardrails and decides whether to fund R2 automation.

sections.heading: Analysis across horizons
sections.body:
Analysis outputs must travel. A delivery finding (auspice bodies ignore email notices 30% of the time) changes an initiative decision (add SMS to auspice contacts in R2) and potentially a strategic assumption (auspice responsiveness). The ABA builds this flow through:

- **Traceability light:** each backlog item links to a capability and outcome.
- **Evidence summaries:** a one-page 'what we learnt' at each review, rolled upward.
- **Shared measures:** the same leading indicators reported at all three horizons.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body:
When several teams work on one product, analysis challenges multiply: competing priorities, cross-team dependencies, inconsistent definitions of data and terms, and features that span teams.

Practices that help:
- **A shared product backlog** with a clear owner for cross-team priority.
- **Feature- or capability-level analysis** held by an ABA working across teams.
- **Shared domain models and glossaries** ('submission date' means one thing everywhere).
- **Joint planning events** to surface dependencies early.
- **Communities of practice** so analysts share techniques and templates.

In the case, scaling would arrive when application, assessment and payments teams all work on time-to-payment. Without a shared definition of 'payment date', each team would report a different number — just as a hospital EMR rollout stalls when wards define 'admission time' differently.

activities.title: Event-analysis map
activities.instructions: For the case, list one event per horizon and describe the analysis input, the decision made and the evidence fed upward.

prompts.label: Delivery event: input · decision · evidence up

activities.title: Scaling risks
activities.instructions: Assume three teams (Applications, Assessment, Payments). Identify three cross-team analysis risks and a practice to mitigate each. Include one shared definition that must be agreed.

participant.aiPrompt: We have [number] teams working on [product]. Their backlogs are: [summaries]. Identify cross-team dependencies, inconsistent terms or data definitions, and features that span teams. Propose a shared glossary of the ten most important terms and an agenda for a joint planning session focused on dependencies.

quiz.q: Which event is the main opportunity to gather evidence about whether an increment moved an indicator?
quiz.why: Reviews inspect the increment with stakeholders.

quiz.q: A delivery finding that changes an initiative decision is an example of…
quiz.why: Evidence travels upward.

quiz.q: At scale, why is a shared glossary important?
opts: Different teams otherwise define key terms and measures differently
quiz.why: e.g. 'payment date' must mean one thing.

takeaways: Know each event's analysis job
Every horizon has events — get into them
Build upward evidence flow deliberately
At scale, shared definitions and dependency analysis are essential

presenter.purpose: Show participants where in the cadence they can influence decisions, and prepare them for scaled environments.
presenter.openingLine: "Show of hands: who's ever been told 'that decision was made at PI planning, you weren't there'? Today is about being in the room — or making sure your analysis is."

beats.label: Hook
beats.notes: Show of hands; collect stories.

beats.label: Delivery events table
beats.notes: Focus on sprint review as the evidence event.

beats.label: Initiative and strategy events
beats.notes: Use the case cadence.

beats.label: Activity 1
beats.notes: Pairs.

beats.label: Across horizons and scaling
beats.notes: Tell the 30% email-ignored story; then scaling practices.

beats.label: Activity 2
beats.notes: Trios.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Harvest shared definitions; bridge to challenges.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Stay framework-neutral: some participants use SAFe, others LeSS or home-grown models. Translate terms rather than debating frameworks. Activity 2's shared definition is usually 'payment date' or 'submission date' — draw out how timestamp sources differ.
presenter.whatGood: Event maps with explicit upward evidence; scaling risks tied to concrete mitigations and at least one shared definition.
presenter.commonFailure: Framework debates hijack the session — fix: park them and ask 'what analysis does this event need, whatever it's called?'
debrief: Which event do you most need to be in?
What shared definition would most help your organisation?
How does evidence currently reach your executives?
presenter.answerKey:
**Event map:** Delivery — sprint review: input is the auspice notification increment and confirmation-rate data; decision is accept and tune reminders; evidence up: 30% of auspice bodies ignore email. Initiative — monthly review: input days-to-payment by tier; decision: add auspice SMS to R2; evidence up: auspice responsiveness assumption weaker than believed. Strategy — quarterly steering: input trajectory vs ≤20 days and guardrails; decision: fund R2 automation or pivot.

**Scaling risks:** inconsistent definition of 'payment date' (agree glossary: date funds are released to the organisation's bank account); Applications ships fields Payments can't consume (shared data model, joint refinement); competing priorities (single product owner for cross-team ordering).

modules.title: Common challenges and competencies
modules.subtitle: What goes wrong, and what the ABA needs to be good at

participant.bigIdea: Agile analysis fails in predictable ways — and the competencies that prevent it can be learnt.
participant.overview: Even well-intentioned agile teams hit recurring analysis problems: backlogs that grow without value, stakeholders who disengage, documentation that is either missing or excessive, and pressure to treat agile as 'faster waterfall'. This session names those challenges, offers practical responses, and then looks at the underlying competencies the guide associates with agile analysis — the mix of thinking, interpersonal and domain capabilities that make an ABA effective.
objectives: Recognise common agile analysis challenges and their causes
Select practical responses to each challenge
Describe the underlying competencies of an effective ABA
Create a personal development plan

keyPoints.title: Challenges are patterns
keyPoints.body: Bloated backlogs, absent stakeholders, documentation extremes, horizon confusion and outcome-less delivery recur everywhere.

keyPoints.title: Respond with principles
keyPoints.body: Each challenge maps to a weak principle — use the principle to choose the fix.

keyPoints.title: Competencies, not just techniques
keyPoints.body: Systems thinking, facilitation, negotiation, adaptability and domain knowledge matter as much as any canvas.

keyPoints.title: Grow deliberately
keyPoints.body: Pick two competencies and practise them in real events with feedback.

sections.heading: Common challenges and responses
sections.body:
| Challenge | Symptom | Likely weak principle | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bloated backlog | Hundreds of items, no clear top ten | Analyse to determine what is valuable | Rank against outcome; archive anything untouched for 90 days |
| Absent stakeholders | Reviews with no business attendees | Stimulate collaboration | Shorter, outcome-focused reviews; go to stakeholders |
| Documentation extremes | Either nothing or 80-page specs | Avoid waste | Document what must outlive the conversation: rules, decisions, models |
| Horizon confusion | Execs debating field names; teams guessing strategy | See the whole | Make the horizon map visible; route questions |
| Output obsession | Velocity celebrated; outcome unmeasured | Deliver value continuously | Report leading indicators at every review |
| Faster waterfall | Fixed scope chopped into sprints | Embrace uncertainty | Re-frame scope as hypotheses with decision points |

sections.heading: Documentation that earns its place
sections.body:
Agile teams still document — selectively. Keep: business rules (e.g. low-risk triage criteria), decisions and their rationale, domain models and glossaries, regulatory traceability (grants guidelines, financial delegations), and examples that serve as tests. Skip: duplicated narrative, speculative detail for work not yet prioritised, and documents nobody reads.

In a regulated environment like public grants administration — or clinical governance in healthcare, or AML/KYC in fintech — traceability to policy and legislation is non-negotiable, but it can be lightweight: a table linking each rule to its authoritative source.

sections.heading: Underlying competencies
sections.body:
| Cluster | Competencies | Agile emphasis |
|---|---|---|
| Analytical thinking | Systems thinking, conceptual thinking, decision-making, creative thinking | Seeing the whole across horizons; framing hypotheses |
| Behavioural | Adaptability, ethics, personal accountability, trustworthiness | Comfort with changing direction on evidence |
| Interaction | Facilitation, negotiation, teaching, teamwork, leadership | Running refinement; coaching the team to analyse |
| Communication | Verbal, written, visual, listening | Concise artefacts; telling the evidence story |
| Business and domain knowledge | Industry, organisation, solution knowledge | Knowing probity, procurement and accessibility constraints |
| Tools and technology | Collaboration and modelling tools, AI assistants | Using AI to draft while retaining judgement |

sections.heading: Agile analysis and AI
sections.body: AI agents can draft story maps, example tables and assumption lists in seconds. That raises the value of the ABA's judgement: knowing which assumption actually matters, which example exposes a real rule, and which output reflects the organisation's context rather than generic patterns. Treat AI output as a first draft from a capable but uninformed colleague: feed it context, challenge it, verify against evidence, and never let it decide.

activities.title: Challenge clinic
activities.instructions: In trios, each person describes a real challenge (2 minutes). The trio identifies the weak principle and proposes a response that can start next sprint.

activities.title: Competency plan
activities.instructions: Rate yourself 1–5 on each competency cluster. Pick two to develop and define a practice opportunity, a feedback source and a 90-day check.

participant.aiPrompt: I'm an agile business analyst. My self-assessment is: [paste ratings]. My current context is: [team, product, organisation]. Suggest a 90-day development plan for my two weakest competencies, with weekly practice opportunities inside normal agile events, how to get feedback, and how I'll know I've improved.

quiz.q: A backlog of 400 items with no clear top ten reflects which weak principle?
opts: Analyse to determine what is valuable
quiz.why: No value-based ordering.

quiz.q: Which documentation should an agile team keep in a regulated setting?
opts: Business rules, decisions, and traceability to legislation
Full 80-page specifications for all future work
quiz.why: Document what must outlive the conversation.

quiz.q: The best stance toward AI-drafted analysis is…
opts: Treat it as a first draft to challenge with context and evidence
quiz.why: The ABA retains judgement.

takeaways: Challenges are predictable — map each to a principle
Document what must outlive the conversation
Competencies outlast techniques
AI raises the premium on judgement

presenter.purpose: Normalise common challenges, give practical responses, and turn learning into a personal development plan.
presenter.openingLine: "Everything we've taught you will meet reality on Monday. So let's bring reality into the room now — your actual challenges, and how to handle them."

beats.label: Hook
beats.notes: Invite one-word challenges in chat.

beats.label: Challenges table
beats.notes: Map chat words to table rows.

beats.label: Documentation that earns its place
beats.notes: Case: statutory traceability table.

beats.label: Activity 1: challenge clinic
beats.notes: Trios; strict 2-minute descriptions.

beats.label: Competencies and AI
beats.notes: Walk clusters; discuss AI as uninformed colleague.

beats.label: Activity 2: competency plan
beats.notes: Solo.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Revisit 1B principle actions — still right?

presenter.facilitationNotes: The challenge clinic can become venting. Keep trios to the structure: describe, diagnose principle, propose a next-sprint response. Revisit the 1B health check actions on the shared board — it closes the loop between mindset and practice.
presenter.whatGood: Responses that are specific, start next sprint and are tied to a principle; development plans with real practice opportunities.
presenter.commonFailure: Responses depend on someone else changing ('management needs to…') — fix: ask 'what can you do in the next event you attend?'
debrief: Which challenge came up most?
Which competency will you practise first?
Does your 1B action still hold?
presenter.answerKey:
**Example clinic result:** Challenge — reviews attended only by the team. Weak principle — stimulate collaboration. Response — cut review to 30 minutes, open with the days-to-payment chart, invite two named regional assessors and one community organisation representative, ask each for one decision-relevant reaction.

**Example competency plan:** Facilitation — run the next two refinements; ask the scrum master for feedback on question quality; 90-day check: team writes examples without prompting. Systems thinking — build a causal loop of grant-payment delays; review with the PO; 90-day check: used in a steering paper.

modules.title: Exercise: technique selection
modules.subtitle: Choose the right technique for the horizon and the question · course close

participant.bigIdea: A good ABA doesn't know every technique — they know which question each one answers.
participant.overview: The final exercise brings the whole course together. You receive analysis scenarios from the running case spanning all three horizons. For each, identify the horizon, the question really being asked, the technique you'd use and the output you'd produce. Then apply the same thinking to your own initiative and commit to your first move on Monday.
objectives: Select techniques appropriate to horizon and question
Justify technique choice against principles
Commit to a first action on your own initiative

keyPoints.title: Question first
keyPoints.body: Clarify the decision before picking a technique.

keyPoints.title: Horizon shapes depth
keyPoints.body: The same technique (e.g. personas) is used lightly at strategy and in detail at delivery.

keyPoints.title: Smallest useful output
keyPoints.body: Choose the technique that produces just enough for the decision.

sections.heading: Technique quick reference
sections.body:
| Horizon | Techniques |
|---|---|
| Strategy | Business model canvas, purpose alignment model, value stream mapping, impact mapping, assumption mapping, real options, Kano analysis |
| Initiative | Story mapping, journey mapping, personas, MVP definition, value modelling, stakeholder mapping, capability mapping |
| Delivery | User stories, specification by example, Given/When/Then, story slicing, lightweight process and data models, storyboarding, backlog refinement |
| All horizons | Retrospectives, hypothesis framing, relative estimation, visual models, prioritisation |

sections.heading: Scenarios
sections.body:
1. The steering committee asks whether to fund automation (R2) now or wait.
2. A tester asks what happens when an organisation submits two applications for the same project.
3. The PO wants to know which applicant groups struggle most with the online form.
4. The Regional Operations Director says assessors won't change processes without KPI changes.
5. The executive asks whether the twenty-day target still makes sense after six months.
6. The team can't agree whether 'submitted' means received or validated.

activities.title: Technique selection
activities.instructions: In groups, for each scenario record: horizon, the real question, chosen technique, output and the principle that justifies the choice.

activities.title: My Monday move
activities.instructions: For your own initiative, name the first analysis move you'll make, at which horizon, with which technique, in which event.

participant.aiPrompt: Here is an analysis request I've received: [paste]. Tell me which planning horizon it belongs to, the real decision behind it, two candidate techniques with pros and cons, and the smallest output that would support the decision. Ask me up to three clarifying questions first if needed.

quiz.q: 'What happens when an organisation submits two applications for the same project?' calls for…
quiz.why: A delivery-level rule clarified through examples.

quiz.q: 'Does the seven-day target still make sense?' belongs to which horizon?
quiz.why: Target-setting is strategic.

quiz.q: The team disagrees on what 'submitted' means. The best technique is…
quiz.why: A shared definition resolves ambiguity.

takeaways: Question first, technique second
Match depth to horizon
Leave with one concrete Monday move

presenter.purpose: Integrate the course through technique selection and close with commitments.
presenter.openingLine: "Six scenarios, three horizons, one case. This is what a normal fortnight looks like for an ABA. Let's see how you'd play it."

beats.label: Brief
beats.notes: Show reference table and scenarios.

beats.label: Group work
beats.notes: Breakouts; broadcast at 12 minutes to move to scenarios 4–6.

beats.label: Debrief scenarios
beats.notes: Rapid round; focus on 1, 4 and 6.

beats.label: Monday move and close
beats.notes: Each participant states their move in one sentence; thank-yous and resources.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Accept multiple valid techniques if justified. Scenario 4 is often answered with 'escalate' — redirect to stakeholder analysis and purpose alignment. Finish on time; the Monday move round is the emotional close, so protect those last ten minutes.
presenter.whatGood: Each scenario has a horizon, a reframed question and a justified technique; every participant leaves with a concrete first move.
presenter.commonFailure: Choosing favourite techniques regardless of question — fix: ask 'what decision does this output support?'
debrief: Which scenario was hardest to place?
What's your Monday move?
What will you tell your manager about this course?
presenter.answerKey:
1 — Strategy/Initiative boundary; question: is MVP evidence strong enough to invest? Technique: real options with MVP results review; output: decision paper with evidence and recommendation. Principle: deliver value continuously / embrace uncertainty.
2 — Delivery; question: what's the duplicate-application rule? Technique: specification by example; output: Given/When/Then table. Principle: get real using examples.
3 — Initiative; question: who is underserved? Technique: personas and journey mapping using application data; output: 2–3 personas (e.g. volunteer-run club, multicultural association, regional Aboriginal community-controlled organisation) with pain points. Principle: think as a customer.
4 — Initiative; question: what drives assessor behaviour? Technique: stakeholder mapping plus purpose alignment, then incentive analysis; output: engagement plan and proposed KPI change. Principle: understand what is doable.
5 — Strategy; question: has evidence changed the bet? Technique: outcome review against leading indicators and assumption map; output: refreshed outcome and assumptions. Principle: see the whole.
6 — Delivery (with cross-horizon impact); question: what does 'submitted' mean? Technique: glossary and lightweight data model; output: agreed definition with timestamp source. Principle: avoid waste.
